title: Minimum Spanning Tree (Kruskal's Algorithm)
oneLiner: Connect every node as cheaply as possible: take edges cheapest-first, skipping any that would close a loop.
keyTakeaway: Sort the edges by weight and walk them in order. Use Union-Find to ask "are these two ends already connected?": if not, take the edge and union them; if so, the edge would make a cycle, so skip it. Stop after n - 1 edges. Fewer than n - 1 means the graph isn't connected.
explanation:
You need to cable six buildings together. Each possible link has a cost, and you want every building reachable from every other for the least total spend. Any cheapest answer will be a tree: a loop always contains an edge you could remove while keeping everything connected. That tree is the minimum spanning tree (MST), and it has exactly n - 1 edges for n nodes.

Kruskal's algorithm is greedy, and here greedy is provably right. Sort all edges from cheapest to most expensive. Go through them in that order; take an edge if its two ends are not yet connected by the edges you've already taken, otherwise skip it. The check "already connected?" is exactly what Union-Find (this track) answers in nearly O(1): find(u) == find(v) means same component. Taking an edge is union(u, v).

In this lesson edges are [u, v, weight] for nodes 0..n-1. Return the total weight of the MST, or -1 if some node can't be reached (you took fewer than n - 1 edges).

Watch the visualization: edges are tried cheapest first; the 4-cost edge from 0 to 1 is skipped because 0 and 1 are already joined through 2.

recognitionSignals: Connect ALL points/nodes with minimum total cost, and any connection pattern is allowed as long as everything ends up connected.
The answer is a set of edges (or its total weight), not a path between two particular nodes.
gotchas: Sort by WEIGHT, not by node number -- the greedy argument only holds cheapest-first.
Check connectivity with Union-Find before taking an edge; taking one between already-connected nodes makes a cycle and overpays.
A disconnected graph has no spanning tree: if you finish with fewer than n - 1 edges, report that (here, -1) instead of a partial sum.
confusableWith: Dijkstra's Algorithm: also weighted edges and greedy, but it finds the shortest PATH from one source. An MST minimizes the total of all edges used; the MST path between two nodes can be longer than their shortest path.
Union-Find (this track) is the building block here -- the MST lesson is Union-Find plus sorting.

complexity.note: Sorting the E edges dominates; the Union-Find checks afterwards are nearly O(1) each. log E and log V differ by at most a factor of 2, so O(E log V) is the same bound. Space is the parent array plus the sorted edge list.

referenceSolutions.python:
def min_spanning_tree_cost(n, edges):
    parent = list(range(n))

    def find(x):
        while parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
            x = parent[x]
        return x

    total = taken = 0
    for u, v, w in sorted(edges, key=lambda e: e[2]):  # cheapest first
        root_u, root_v = find(u), find(v)
        if root_u == root_v:  # already connected: this edge would close a loop
            continue
        parent[root_u] = root_v
        total += w
        taken += 1
    return total if taken == n - 1 else -1
